query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A single thermal annealing step that promotes controlled surface segregation of trace platinum (Pt) in the near‐equiatomic multi‐principal alloy catalyst will form an atomically dispersed, Pt‐enriched nanoshell that simultaneously improves low‐temperature oxidation activity, enhances resistance to poisoning (e.g., by H2O and NO), and boosts lifetime durability—all while using only minimal Pt.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic, multi‐principal automotive alloy catalyst with uniformly distributed elements and very low platinum-group-metal content.
generation.intervention: Apply a carefully optimized thermal annealing treatment designed to drive Pt atoms to segregate onto the particle surfaces, resulting in a conformal, atomically dispersed Pt-enriched nanoshell over the alloy catalyst.
generation.conditions: Simulated automotive exhaust environments that include transient, low-temperature operation (below 150 °C), exposure to common poisons such as H2O and NO, and accelerated thermal aging (e.g., around 14 hours under cycling oxidizing/reducing conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable, Pt-enriched surface layer (nanoshell) stabilized by the high-entropy configuration of the underlying alloy, which mitigates nanoparticle sintering and structural degradation.
generation.mechanism: The atomically dispersed Pt sites on the catalyst surface provide favorable active centers for low-temperature oxidation with reduced CO or other intermediate binding strength (minimizing poisoning). Meanwhile, the high-entropy substrate resists sintering and maintains structural integrity over prolonged aging cycles, ensuring durability without increasing overall PGM content.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified catalyst, the annealed catalyst is expected to exhibit a lower onset temperature for complete oxidation (i.e., a reduction in T50 and T100), enhanced performance in the presence of water and NO (less deactivation), and improved long-term durability under simulated exhaust operating conditions.
generation.baseline: The unmodified near‐equiatomic alloy catalyst shows higher oxidation temperatures and greater susceptibility to deactivation under poisoning and thermal aging conditions.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the intervention is dependent on maintaining the trace Pt content at very low levels and on the precise control of annealing parameters; if the parameters are not optimized, there is a risk of over-enrichment of the surface or unwanted phase separation, negating the desired effects.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the performance gains (in terms of temperature reduction and durability improvement) is uncertain and will depend on the optimal distribution of Pt achieved during annealing, requiring further experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of near‐equiatomic multi‐principal alloy catalysts with identical overall compositions but subject one batch to the optimized thermal annealing treatment and leave the other unmodified. Expose both batches to simulated automotive exhaust conditions with transient low temperatures, water vapor, and NO, and perform accelerated aging tests. Conduct surface compositional analyses (e.g., XPS, STEM-EDS) to confirm Pt surface enrichment in the annealed sample.
measurements: CO oxidation conversion temperatures (T50 and T100) measured under both dry and humid conditions
Catalytic activity retention over a prolonged aging test (e.g., percentage drop in activity after 14 hours)
Surface composition and distribution of Pt via XPS and/or STEM-EDS
Poisoning resistance assessed by catalytic performance in the presence of H2O and NO
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the annealed catalyst does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in low-temperature oxidation activity, resistance to poisoning, or durability compared to the unmodified catalyst, or if the annealing treatment leads to an undesirable increase in platinum-group-metal use or catalyst deactivation.

The catalytic oxidation of CO is a key heterogeneous gas‐solid process and a valuable probe for studying catalyst structure, metal‒support interactions, adsorption‐desorption behavior, and reaction mechanisms.[  ] The catalytic activity, stability, and water tolerance of the Pt/HEO for CO oxidation were systematically evaluated. As shown in Figure 4a, the Pt/HEO catalyst achieved full CO conversion at 195 °C, significantly lower than the 430 °C required by HEO nanofibers alone (Figure S33, Supporting Information), highlighting the critical role of Pt nanoparticles. Interestingly, the catalytic performance of the Pt/HEO improved substantially after thermal aging. After aging in N2 at 700 °C, the conversion temperature dropped to 182 °C. cited_evidence.text: These results underline the exceptional thermal stability of Pt nanoparticles, which is attributed to the high‐entropy effect. As shown in Figure 4g, the Pt/HEO‐850 °C catalyst demonstrated excellent stability during CO oxidation at 210 °C, maintaining consistent activity over 338 h with ignorable decline (Table S3, Supporting Information). The Pt/HEO‐850 °C demonstrates a slight decline (2.4%) in the 30‐h running with a low deactivation rate constant (k d) of 3.2 × 10−3 h−1, compared with recent Pt‐based catalysts (Figure 4h).[  ] This result exceeds the thermal stability conventional catalysts, showcasing its superior sinter‐resistance. To simulate hydrothermal conditions, vapor was introduced during testing, and even after 35 consecutive cycles, ignorable performance declines were observed (Figure 4i). In the 36th cycle, the porous structure remained intact, with the Pt nanoparticle size increasing only by 0.1–2.7 nm (Figures S36 and S37, Supporting Information). The durability of Pt/HEO in moisture‐rich environments, such as automotive exhaust systems, underscores its potential as a highly reliable catalyst for CO oxidation. As the first order of approximation, we introduced a doping Co/Ni/Bi/Sn atom onto Pt(111) surface to evaluate the individual contribution from each kind of element in HEASA-Pt (Supplementary Fig. 2). Co and Bi have been reported to promote electron transfer in catalysts, lowering the oxidation energy barrier of *CO and facilitating the MOR,. Ni and Sn can act as oxyphilic elements to enhance the adsorption of OH−, thereby accelerating the oxidation of *CO and improving the anti-CO poisoning ability of catalysts,. The effects of the alloying elements could be separated into two categories. On the one hand, modification of the coordination environment around Pt influences its reactivity. As shown in Fig. 1b, doping with a Bi or Sn atom weakened CO binding on adjacent Pt sites, suppressing CO poisoning, which is a well-known degradation mechanism of Pt-based MOR catalysts.
